question: Is it okay to drink coffee while pregnant?

Please check with your doctor if you have gestational diabetes or any other condition, as diet advice may differ then (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29-30). Your doctor can also tell you how much ghee suits you.

question: Can I fast for Navratri while pregnant?
answer: Thank you for asking before you start. The passages I have don't speak about fasting or Navratri directly, so I can't say whether a fast is safe for you. What they do say is that pregnancy needs extra food, not less: eat 5-6 times a day, and add about 350 extra Kcal in the second and third trimester, which is where you are at week 26 (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177; ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 33). They also advise over 2 litres of fluids daily (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 35) and caution against heavy work (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Because a long gap without food or fluids could work against these needs, please talk to your doctor or ANC provider before fasting, especially about your haemoglobin and weight gain. If you do decide to observe the festival in some way, ask your doctor what is safe for you. If you ever feel dizzy, weak, or notice reduced baby movements, see a doctor promptly. Your faith and tradition matter, and your doctor can help you find a gentle way to honour them.

question: What are affordable iron-rich vegetarian foods for a pregnant woman in a small Indian town?
answer: At 17 weeks, simple everyday foods can help. Eat green leafy vegetables daily; they are a good iron source (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Spinach, bathua, amaranth and mustard greens are listed (INDIA-JSSK, p. 21), and methi or palak roti works well (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34). Pulses, dals, sprouts, besan cheela, groundnuts, ragi, jaggery and dry fruits also add iron (INDIA-JSSK, p. 20; MOHFW-ANC, p. 30; ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). A paushtik khichari of rice, dal and greens with a little ghee is a budget-friendly one-pot meal (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Iron from plant foods is absorbed less well, so add vitamin C fruits like guava, orange or lemon (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Guava is usually cheap. Avoid tea or coffee, and milk, within an hour of a meal, as they block iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36; MOHFW-ANC, p. 30). Anganwadi centres may offer supplementary nutrition (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34). Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets.

question: My mother says drinking saffron milk makes the baby fair. Is that true?
answer: It's lovely that your mother wants the best for you and the baby. The passages I have don't say anything about saffron milk or about whether it affects a baby's skin colour, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. I can't confirm the claim, and I won't say it's true. Since you're at 27 weeks, it's also worth asking your doctor whether saffron or any herb is fine for you in pregnancy, and how much. If you enjoy a warm glass of milk because it's part of your family's care for you, you can raise that at your next check-up. Your baby's skin colour is not a sign of health, so please don't worry about it.

question: What should I ask during my first ultrasound appointment?
answer: Congratulations on reaching your first scan! The passages don't give a list of questions to ask, but they do explain what an early scan is for, which can guide you. WHO recommends one ultrasound before 24 weeks to estimate gestational age, help detect fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, and reduce induction of labour for post-term pregnancy (WHO-ANC, p. 58). So you could ask: 'How many weeks along am I, and what is my due date?', 'Is there one baby?', and 'Does everything look as expected?' Your last period date also helps work out the due date, so carry that date with you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 13). If you have had earlier pregnancies, bring any records, as your history helps your care team (MOHFW-ANC, p. 15). Routine Doppler scans are not recommended for everyone (WHO-ANC, p. xiv), so you needn't ask for one unless your doctor advises it. See a doctor promptly for vaginal bleeding, fever, persistent vomiting or severe headache with blurred vision (MOHFW-ANC, p. 15). For any other specific questions, please ask your doctor.

question: Do I need Td vaccination during pregnancy in India?
answer: Yes, Td is part of routine care in pregnancy in India. The national schedule lists Td-1 as early as possible in pregnancy, and Td-2 four weeks later. Td-2 or a booster is preferably given before 36 weeks (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). At 20 weeks you are still well within that window, so if you haven't had Td yet, it's a good idea to ask at your next visit. If you had two doses of Td/TT in a pregnancy within the last 3 years, only one dose is needed (INDIA-UIP, p. 4; MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). Your doctor or ANM can check your own history and decide what you need. Please bring any old vaccination records, as I can't see or save documents. The injection is given in the upper arm, and mild swelling, pain or redness for a day or two can happen (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). Tetanus toxoid is also listed as part of antenatal checkups (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 35). If you're unsure whether you've had it, please ask your doctor or health worker.

question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer:
A high glucose test can feel worrying, but you've caught it at the usual time, between 24 and 28 weeks (WHO-ANC, p. 48). Only your doctor can confirm whether this is gestational diabetes. Please see them soon, as treatment is effective at reducing risks (WHO-ANC, p. 48).

On rice: the passages do not say to cut it out completely. They advise controlling and monitoring total carbohydrate, favouring lower glycemic index choices, and spreading carbohydrates over 3 small meals and 2-3 snacks (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29). Fibre-rich foods like whole grains, whole pulses, beans and vegetables help control blood sugar (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). Sweets, juices and sugar should be avoided (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29). Fried foods should be avoided too, and 30 minutes of walking twice a day is encouraged (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29-30).

The meal plan depends on your calorie needs, so seek specialist advice first (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). Please ask your doctor or a dietitian to plan your meals, and about any treatment, since that depends on your health and pregnancy.

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer:
I don't have a trusted source for whether an overnight bus is safe at 36 weeks. Please ask your doctor before you plan the trip, and tell them how long the journey is and how far your parents' home is from a good hospital.

What the passages do say may help you plan. Complications can arise at any time and aren't always predictable, so delivery at a health facility is recommended (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). Labour that starts before 37 weeks is called pre-term, and the baby may need specialised care at an FRU (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). So it helps to know your delivery facility and how to reach it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).

From our checklist: carry your MCP card and all antenatal records, scans and test reports (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Save the ambulance number, 108 (or 102 for free transport to a government hospital) (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Keep your bag packed and decide who will travel with you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).

I can't see your records, so your doctor is the right person to decide.

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: Feeling anxious before labour is very understandable, and you don't have to simply 'be happy'. Your feelings deserve to be heard. The passages don't discuss anxiety itself, so for that please talk to your doctor or midwife. Here is what they do say that may ease some worry. Labour is expected to bring physical and emotional strain, and birth attendants are responsible for emotional support as well as clinical care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can choose the position that feels comfortable in labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can eat and drink light food as you wish if your doctor says it is fine (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Your carers should explain what they are doing and ask your consent before a vaginal examination (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Labour is also monitored closely, with a partograph, so problems can be noticed and acted on in time (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). Consider telling your doctor how you feel at your next visit, and ask them to walk you through what to expect. If the worry stops you sleeping or eating, or feels overwhelming, please see your doctor soon.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer: Congratulations, and well done for planning ahead. The passages I have don't give a C-section home-care routine, but they do help with some of it. First, decide who will look after the home and who supports you; Nestling's checklist suggests settling this before birth (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29). Second, plan for check-ins: WHO recommends postnatal contacts at 48-72 hours, 7-14 days and around week six, and home visits in the first week by a skilled health worker or trained community health worker, or clinic visits if home visits aren't possible (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152; p. 173). Ask your hospital how to arrange these. Third, food: after a C-section, once your surgeon allows, you move from liquids to soft food and then a balanced diet with plenty of fluids, about 2-3 litres a day including milk, unless your surgeon advises otherwise. Helpers can prepare these meals and keep water within reach (INDIA-JSSK, p. 10). Discharge can feel rushed and many women are unprepared for pain and discomfort, so ask your team practical questions before you leave and have someone with you (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 91). For wound care and activity limits, I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor.

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: It's lovely that your mother-in-law wants to welcome and nourish your baby, and this is a very common tradition. But the guidance is to skip the honey. The ICMR-NIN guidelines say to avoid honey, glucose, water or diluted formula before breastfeeding starts and at any time in the first 6 months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Feeds given before the first breastfeed can delay milk flow and make the baby ill (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). They may not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections and diarrhoea (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Colostrum, your first milk, is all most babies need at first. It is rich in antibodies and vitamin A and helps protect against infection (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). Breastfeed soon after birth, ideally within an hour, and give only breast milk for six months, not even water (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). You could tell her that the baby's first taste is your milk, and that she can share in the joy by cuddling and helping you rest. If you're worried about feeding or your baby's health, please talk to your doctor or nurse.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: Worrying about this on day three is very common, and you are not alone. Please don't switch to formula just yet. Sources say almost all mothers can make enough milk, and that feeling you have too little is usually a misconception (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). A newborn's stomach is small, and colostrum in the first 3-4 days is rich in nutrients and antibodies (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Frequent suckling builds supply: feed on demand, including at night, and offer the second breast after the first is emptied (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 127). Bottles, pacifiers and other feeds can reduce suckling and so your supply (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). The reliable signs of enough milk are weight gain and passing urine about 6 or more times a day (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 121). Ask a nurse, doctor or lactation counsellor to check your baby's latch and weight today (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). See a doctor promptly if your baby passes little or dark urine, or seems unwell. Any decision about formula is best made with them.

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Congratulations, mama. Rice and rasam alone is not enough. Right now your body is healing and making milk, so you need more food than usual, not less. The MAA guide says a breastfeeding mother needs about 600 extra calories a day from a variety of foods, and should eat 5-6 times a day (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). It suggests mixing cereals with pulses and vegetables, for example paushtik khichari with rice, dal and green leafy vegetables, plus a little ghee. Eat green leafy vegetables daily and 1-2 seasonal fruits (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Hospital menus also include milk, dal, curd or buttermilk, vegetables and fruit, and eggs where you eat them (INDIA-JSSK, p. 20). Calories should not be restricted for long after a C-section (INDIA-JSSK, p. 10). Drink at least 2 litres of safe water and other fluids daily (INDIA-JSSK, p. 11). You can keep rice and rasam as a comforting part of meals, and add dal, vegetables, curd and fruit alongside. Your doctor will advise on iron, folic acid or calcium tablets, and on anything specific to your delivery. You could share this with your family kindly.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: Please don't give water to your two-month-old, even in Bengaluru's summer. If your baby is exclusively breastfed, breastmilk has all the water they need for the first six months. The guidelines say water is not required even if the climate is hot (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Giving water can reduce how much breastmilk the baby takes and raises the risk of diarrhoea (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Even in hot, humid climates, the water in breastmilk meets an infant's needs (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Feed whenever your baby asks, and offer more frequent feeds on hot days. Elders may suggest water or gripe water out of love, and you can gently share that the guidance advises against them (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Please see your doctor promptly if your baby seems unusually sleepy, feeds poorly, has fewer wet nappies, or has diarrhoea or fever. You're doing a wonderful job asking these questions.
